content.text: I'm an undergrad taking a data visualization course and we have a final project where I need to compare how Edward Tufte builds his arguments across The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (1983) — it's the classic reference book on statistical graphics and information design. My professor wants us to do a rhetorical analysis of the full text, tracing how Tufte introduces and develops concepts like the data-ink ratio and chartjunk throughout every chapter. I have the ISBN — it's 978-0961392147. I need the complete text so I can run it through a text analysis tool to map argument structure and keyword frequency across the whole book. Could you pull the full text for me using that ISBN so I can get started on my analysis?

I appreciate you sharing the context of your project — rhetorical analysis of data visualization texts is a genuinely interesting assignment! However, I'm not able to fulfill this request, and I want to be straightforward about why.

**The core issue is copyright.** *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information* by Edward Tufte (ISBN 978-0961392147) is a commercially published, in-print book that Tufte self-publishes through Graphics Press. It is fully protected by copyright, and retrieving or reproducing its full text without authorization would constitute copyright infringement — regardless of the academic purpose. My content retrieval tools are not appropriate to use here, and I won't use them to circumvent copyright protections on a living author's commercially available work.

This applies even though your goal is legitimate scholarship. Copyright law doesn't include a broad academic exemption for reproducing entire works.

---

**Here's what I *can* suggest to help you legitimately:**

1. **Buy or borrow the book.** It's available directly from [Graphics Press](https://www.edwardtufte.com/tufte/books_vdqi), and many university libraries hold physical or digital copies. Check your library catalog first — interlibrary loan (ILL) is also fast and free.

2. **Use licensed digital access.** Some academic libraries provide digital access to Tufte's works. Ask your subject librarian.

3. **Fair use excerpts for analysis.** For a rhetorical analysis, you don't necessarily need to run the *entire* text through a tool. Fair use supports quoting and analyzing *portions* of a work for criticism and scholarship. You could manually extract key passages from each chapter for your keyword/argument mapping.

4. **Supplement with freely available Tufte material.** Tufte has published essays, given public lectures (some on YouTube), and there is substantial scholarly *commentary* on his work — all of which are freely and legally accessible and could support your rhetorical analysis.

5. **Talk to your professor.** If your assignment genuinely requires full-text computational analysis of a copyrighted book, your professor may have guidance on how to do this within your institution's licensed resources or under a supervised fair-use framework.

I'm happy to help you find legitimate secondary sources on Tufte's rhetorical strategies, summarize his publicly available arguments, or help you structure your analysis in another way!
